chapters.name: Chapter 1: What makes a good educational campaign

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What an educational campaign is
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Tell an educational campaign from a regular ad.
This lesson builds toward: Given examples of posts, you will explain how an educational campaign differs from a regular ad, naming the four parts of a good campaign: one learning goal, accurate facts, a simple action and honesty about who pays.
A regular ad says "buy this". An educational campaign says "here is something useful to know or do". Brands use athletes in these campaigns because athletes are trusted by young people and families.
Examples of campaign topics: learning to swim and water safety, recognizing concussion signs, reading every day, staying hydrated, saving money, online safety, or mental health awareness.
Good campaigns have one learning goal, accurate facts from trusted sources, a simple action people can take, and honesty about who is paying for it.
Words to know:
- Educational campaign: a series of messages that teaches people something useful, often supported by a brand or nonprofit.
- Learning goal: the one thing you want your audience to know or do after the campaign.
Try it now: Find one educational campaign you have seen with an athlete or brand. Write its learning goal, the action it asked for, and whether it said who paid for it.
You can now tell an educational campaign from a regular ad and name what makes it good.

check.q: What does an educational campaign say?
options: "Here is something useful to know or do"
check.why: A regular ad says buy this; an educational campaign teaches something useful.

check.q: A brand offers you a "campaign" that is just discount codes with no lesson. What is it?
check.why: With no learning goal or useful action, it is a regular ad.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Choosing your cause
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick one cause that fits your story and your audience.
This lesson builds toward: Given causes connected to your life, you will choose one cause and write one learning goal for your audience, with a two-sentence story connection and a goal that says who will know or do what.
The strongest campaigns come from real life. Did a coach teach you about concussions after a teammate got hurt? Did reading help you stay eligible? Did learning to budget your NIL money change things? Your story makes people listen.
Pick a cause that also fits your audience. Younger fans and their parents may care about safety and reading; college peers may care about money skills and mental health.
Write one learning goal: "After my campaign, middle-school players will know three signs of a concussion and to tell a coach right away."
Step by step:
- List three causes connected to your life.
- Mark which fits your audience best.
- Write your story connection in two sentences.
- Write one learning goal.
Words to know:
- Cause: an issue or goal you care about and want to help with.
- Authentic: real and true to who you are.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to help you list causes connected to your sport and life. Pick one and write your two-sentence story and one learning goal.
You can now choose an authentic cause and write a clear learning goal.

check.q: Where do the strongest campaign causes come from?
Your fans are mostly middle-school players and their parents. Which cause fits best?
check.why: Younger fans and their parents may care about safety topics like concussions.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Getting the facts right
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check every fact in your campaign against an official or expert source.
This lesson builds toward: Given the facts you want to share, you will check each fact against an official or expert source and record it on a fact sheet, with a link and date for every fact and any fact you cannot confirm removed.
If you teach something wrong, people can get hurt, and your reputation and your partner's suffer. Every fact needs a trusted source.
Use official and expert sources: government health and safety agencies (for example the CDC's HEADS UP concussion pages), national organizations, and experts like athletic trainers, doctors, teachers or financial counselors. Ask an AI assistant to explain a topic simply, then confirm each fact on the source itself.
Keep a fact sheet: each fact, the source link, and the date you checked it. Teach general awareness and point people to professionals for personal advice.
Step by step:
- List the facts you want to share.
- Find an official or expert source for each.
- Write the link and the date you checked.
- Remove any fact you cannot confirm.
- Point people to professionals for personal advice.
Words to know:
- Official source: information from a government agency or the organization in charge of the topic.
- Fact sheet: a list of your facts with their sources and dates checked.
Official sources:
- CDC: HEADS UP (concussion awareness)
Try it now: Write three facts for your campaign. Find an official or expert source for each and build your fact sheet with links and dates.
You can now check campaign facts against official sources and keep a fact sheet.

check.q: What goes on a fact sheet?
options: Each fact, its source link and the date you checked it
check.why: A fact sheet keeps each fact with its source and the date checked.

check.q: A follower asks you what to do about their own injury. What do you do?
options: Ask an AI and repost the answer
Point them to a doctor or athletic trainer
check.why: Teach general awareness and point people to professionals for personal advice.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Planning three posts with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draft a three-post campaign plan with AI and edit it.
This lesson builds toward: Using your fact sheet and an AI assistant, you will create a three-post plan: why it matters, what to know and take action, with a hook, main points and a call to action for each post, only facts from your fact sheet, and a hopeful tone.
Three posts are enough for a focused campaign: 1. Why it matters (your story). 2. What to know or do (the main lesson). 3. Take action (a simple step, like "share this with your team" or "take the free training").
Ask an AI assistant: "Here is my cause, learning goal, story and fact sheet. Plan three short posts: why it matters, what to know, take action. Give a hook, the main points and a call to action for each. Only use facts from my fact sheet."
Edit for your voice and check every fact against your fact sheet again. Keep it hopeful and practical, not scary.
Step by step:
- Paste your cause, goal, story and fact sheet.
- Ask for three posts: why, what, action.
- Check each fact against your fact sheet.
- Edit into your voice.
- Make the tone hopeful and practical.
Words to know:
- Call to action: the simple step you ask people to take.
- Tone: the feeling of your message, like hopeful or serious.
Try it now: Use AI to draft your three-post plan from your fact sheet. Edit it and check each fact again.
You can now plan a focused three-post campaign with AI and keep the facts accurate.

check.q: What is post 2 of the campaign about?
options: What to know or do: the main lesson
check.why: The three posts are why it matters, what to know, and take action.

check.q: AI's draft adds a statistic that is not on your fact sheet. What do you do?
options: Remove it or confirm it on an official source first
Credit the AI as the source
check.why: Only use facts from your fact sheet.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Pitching a brand or nonprofit partner
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short pitch to a brand or nonprofit that fits your cause.
This lesson builds toward: Given partners who already care about your cause, you will write a short pitch to one brand or nonprofit, under 150 words, with your cause, story, goal, plan, audience and a clear ask, and NIL rules checked.
Partners can add reach, money or resources. Look for ones that already care about your cause: a swim school for water safety, a library or bookstore for reading, a local credit union for money skills, a sports medicine clinic for injury awareness. Nonprofits may welcome a volunteer partnership.
A pitch shows your cause, your story, your learning goal, your three-post plan and your audience. Ask for something clear: sharing the posts, supplying materials, or sponsoring the campaign.
Use AI to draft it, then make it personal. Under 18? Involve a parent or guardian. Student-athletes: check your school's and state's NIL rules before accepting any pay or products.
Step by step:
- List three partners who already care about your cause.
- Write what you will ask for.
- Use AI to draft a pitch under 150 words.
- Personalize it.
- Check NIL rules before accepting pay or products.
Words to know:
- Partner: a brand or nonprofit that works with you on the campaign.
- Nonprofit: an organization that works for a cause instead of profit.
Official sources:
- NCAA: Name, Image and Likeness
Try it now: Pick one partner and write a pitch under 150 words with AI help. Have a coach or parent read it.
You can now pitch a brand or nonprofit partner for your campaign.

check.q: Which partner fits a water safety campaign?
check.why: Look for partners that already care about your cause.

check.q: A partner offers you free gear for your campaign, and you are a student-athlete. What do you do first?
options: Post about it without telling anyone
Check your school's and state's NIL rules
check.why: Check NIL rules before accepting any pay or products.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Disclosure, honesty and measuring impact
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Disclose brand support clearly and measure whether people learned.
This lesson builds toward: For a campaign with any brand support, you will write a clear disclosure for each post and choose two ways to measure learning, with the disclosure near the start, no claims beyond your fact sheet, and results shared with your partner.
If a brand pays you or gives you anything for the campaign, the FTC says to disclose it clearly in each post, near the start: "Paid partnership with [brand]" or "Thanks to [brand] for supporting this campaign". In videos, say it and show it.
Only say what you believe and what your fact sheet supports. Do not let a partner add claims you cannot back up, especially health claims.
Measure learning, not just likes: count shares, saves, comments with questions, people who took the action (like signing up for training), or run a two-question poll at the end. Share results with your partner.
Step by step:
- Add a clear disclosure in each sponsored post.
- Check every claim against your fact sheet.
- Pick two impact measures.
- Run a short poll after post 3.
- Send results to your partner.
Words to know:
- Disclosure: a clear statement that a brand paid or supported you.
- Impact: the real change your campaign made, like people learning or acting.
Official sources:
- FTC: Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers
Try it now: Final task: put together your campaign plan with learning goal, three posts, fact sheet, call to action, partner pitch, disclosure wording and the person you checked NIL rules with.
You can now run an honest educational campaign with clear disclosure and measure its impact.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Cause and learning goal No clear goal, or the cause does not fit the audience. One cause with a story connection and one learning goal that says who will know or do what. The goal is measurable and matches the impact measures chosen. Fact sheet Facts without sources, or facts that could not be confirmed are kept. Every fact has an official or expert source link and the date checked. An expert such as an athletic trainer or teacher has reviewed the facts. Three-post plan Fewer than three posts, or posts missing a hook or call to action. Why, what and action posts, each with a hook, main points and call to action, using only fact-sheet facts. The tone is hopeful and practical and each post points to a professional or free resource. Partner pitch No clear ask, or the partner does not fit the cause. Under 150 words to a fitting partner with cause, story, goal, plan, audience and a clear ask. Personalized with a true reason for choosing that partner and a parent involved where needed. Disclosure and rules No disclosure plan, or NIL rules not checked. A clear disclosure for each post and the person at school or state who confirmed NIL rules. Also names two impact measures and how results will be shared with the partner. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Where should a disclosure go in a sponsored campaign post?
options: Near the start of each post
At the end of many hashtags
check.why: The FTC says disclose clearly in each post, near the start.

check.q: Your campaign got many likes. How do you know if people learned?
options: Run a short poll and count people who took the action
